generatedProse.concept-context: In psychology, a proposal is a framework of questions that turns an interest into a study a supervisor or ethics panel can judge. The questions narrow a broad area, say 'stress and memory', into a specific, answerable one: which population, which manipulation, which measure, over what period. Freshness, not total originality, is the test: a familiar effect examined in a new population, or with a better-controlled design, is fresh enough to be worth doing.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two psychology students draft a proposal from the same broad interest in stress and memory.

Tom writes that the project will study how stress affects memory, because the topic is important and widely discussed, and that he will read around it before deciding on a design. The area is named, but nothing is narrowed. It gives no specific question, no population, no measure and no design. A reader cannot tell what study Tom would actually run, or why this one rather than any other.

Amara drives the same interest through questions. The broad area becomes one specific question: does acute stress impair recall in first-year students more than in final-year students? She says why the comparison matters, summarises what is known and what is not, and sets a workable design against it. The focus is not wholly new, but it is fresh: this comparison, with this measure, has not been run before.

Both began with the same interest. Only Amara built a framework of questions that turned it into a study.
generatedProse.summary: In psychology, a research proposal is a framework of questions that narrows a broad area into a specific, answerable study and shows its freshness rather than claiming total originality. You can now explain how the questions build the framework, recognise the move from a general area to a specific design, and choose the question that sharpens a topic. The final lesson turns to the report that presents a completed study.

check.body: In the worked example, what did Amara do that turned a broad interest into a study?

items.text: She drove the topic through questions into a specific, fresh comparison with a workable design.
She promised to read around the topic before choosing a design.
She chose a question that was entirely original and had never been studied.
She named the broad area and explained that it was important.

feedback.correct: That's right. Amara narrowed the interest through questions into a fresh, workable comparison.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Amara DID to the topic, beyond naming it or promising to read.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara turned the interest into a study by driving it through questions into a specific, fresh comparison with a design. Reading around it, claiming originality or calling it important do not make a study.
